intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. Each note explains a slide, tells you what to remember and warns you where people slip. Work the examples in pencil, answer the recall questions without looking, and write your own notes in the margins.

sections.title: What Is MEL and Why It Matters
sections.big_idea: MEL is **one system**: monitoring tracks delivery, evaluation judges change, and learning turns both into decisions.
in_plain_words: Monitoring tells you what was done and whether it went to plan. Evaluation asks whether the programme worked, for whom and why. Learning feeds both back into decisions. Take any one away and the others stall: data with no judgement, judgement with no data, or reports nobody acts on.

The results chain gives the system its shape. Inputs become activities, activities become outputs, and outputs lead to outcomes and impact. **Monitoring watches the first half, where the programme is in control.** Evaluation looks at the second half, where change shows up slowly. Mixing up outputs and outcomes is the commonest slip.

diagram.caption: the results chain, left half monitored, right half evaluated

key_terms.meaning: Continuous tracking of activities and outputs, mainly for management.
Periodic assessment of effectiveness, efficiency, relevance and impact.
Feeding evidence back into decisions to improve programmes.
A direct product of activities, within programme control.
A medium-term change in knowledge, behaviour or conditions.
Names each indicator, source, tool, owner and frequency.

worked_example.title: Sort the statements and size the budget
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a programme with a Rs 50 lakh budget (50 in lakh units) trains farmers, and the team must also set a MEL budget using the deck's 5 to 10% norm.
steps: '500 farmers trained' counts what the programme produced, so it is an output.
'Farmers adopt climate-resilient varieties' is a change in practice, so it is an outcome.
'Reduced rural poverty' is a long-term change in lives, so it is impact.
MEL at 5% of the budget: 50 × 0.05 = 2.5 lakh.
MEL at 10% of the budget: 50 × 0.1 = 5 lakh.
worked_example.answer: Output, outcome, impact in that order; the MEL budget runs from Rs 2.5 lakh to Rs 5 lakh.

mistakes: Reporting outputs as proof of change. A training count shows activity, and the 'so what?' test pushes you towards the outcome.
Treating monitoring, evaluation and learning as three separate jobs. The value comes from the feedback between them.
Adding MEL after problems appear. The deck says retrofit MEL is consistently worse than MEL designed at the start.
Designing the system for donors alone. It then yields data that looks good and teaches little.

recall.q: What does 'M' in MEL stand for and who is it mainly for?
recall.a: Monitoring, the continuous tracking of activities and outputs, mainly for management.

recall.q: Name the four functions of MEL given on slide 5.
recall.a: Accountability, learning, management, and advocacy and influence.

recall.q: Which parts of the results chain does monitoring usually track?
recall.a: Inputs, activities and outputs.

recall.q: What share of programme budget does the deck give as the MEL norm?
recall.a: 5 to 10%, up to 12 to 15% where learning ambitions are high.

recall.q: What does the 'so what?' test do?
recall.a: It keeps pushing an indicator up the chain until you reach fundamental change in people's lives, which is the impact level.

sections.title: Theory of Change
sections.big_idea: A ToC is a **testable hypothesis** about how change happens, and its weak point is the assumption behind each arrow.
in_plain_words: A Theory of Change says how and why activities should lead to outcomes and impact. The simplest test is if, then, because. If we do this, then that happens, because something is true about people or the setting. The because is the assumption, and it is the part programmes leave unwritten.

Most failures come from **untested assumptions about people**: that women control their savings, that farmers can get credit, that a community will keep a pump running. Build the ToC with staff and communities, start from the problem, stress-test every arrow, and revisit it each year. Complex problems need loops and several pathways.

key_terms.meaning: A condition that must hold for a causal step to work.
The theory of how change happens, such as incentives or norms.
The explicit steps between activity and impact.
What the programme will and will not address.
One with feedback loops and unpredictable outcomes.
Asking what must be true for each arrow to hold.

worked_example.title: Audit one arrow
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's example: a savings programme assumes women will use the account once it is open.
steps: Write the claim: if we open accounts, then women save, because they control household finances.
Name the assumption: women control household finances.
Classify it using the table: this is a social norm assumption.
Choose a test from the table: formative research, a KAP survey or FGDs.
Decide what you will do if the test says no: change the design or add work with husbands.
worked_example.answer: The assumption is untested and social; test it with formative research before relying on it.

mistakes: Writing the ToC alone for a funding proposal. The deck says such a ToC has little value.
Listing outputs as outcomes, for example '200 women form SHGs'.
Stopping at individual behaviour change with no path to systemic change.
Leaving assumptions blank or writing 'no major assumptions'.

recall.q: What does the 'because' in if-then-because represent?
recall.a: The assumption that must hold for the step to follow.

recall.q: Which comes first, the ToC or the logframe?
recall.a: The ToC. The logframe turns it into a planning matrix.

recall.q: Name two of the seven things a good ToC includes.
recall.a: Any two of: problem analysis, change hypothesis, causal pathways, assumptions, boundaries, stakeholders, preconditions.

recall.q: Why does a linear ToC struggle with complex problems?
recall.a: Because outcomes can be non-linear and emergent, with feedback loops and several pathways.

recall.q: How often should a ToC be revisited?
recall.a: At least annually, or sooner when monitoring shows a step is not working.

sections.title: Results Frameworks & Logframes
sections.big_idea: The logframe links each level of result to **indicators, sources and assumptions**, and it works only if the assumptions are real.
in_plain_words: The logframe is a four by four matrix. Rows run from goal down to activities, and columns give indicators, means of verification and assumptions. Read down for vertical logic and along for horizontal logic. It was built for USAID in 1969 and is still the most common format, and the most misused.

Other formats suit other purposes, from USAID results frameworks to Outcome Harvesting. The results matrix adds baseline, target and timeline columns. **A baseline collected before the programme is non-negotiable**, because without it you cannot show change. Treat any framework as provisional and review it at midterm.

diagram.caption: each level needs indicators, sources and assumptions

key_terms.meaning: A 4×4 planning matrix of results, indicators, sources and assumptions.
The named data source for each indicator.
The starting value of an indicator, measured before the programme.
A qualitative marker of progress, such as groups functional.
A quantitative level for an indicator by a date.
Too many indicators, leaving no time to analyse.

worked_example.title: Read a results matrix row
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's matrix. Outcome: average farm income rises from Rs 42,000 to Rs 58,000 by Year 3. Impact: households below the poverty line fall from 42% to 32%.
steps: Income gain in rupees: 58,000 − 42,000 = 16,000.
Income gain as a share of the baseline: 16,000 ÷ 42,000 = 38.1%.
Poverty target in points: 42 − 32 = 10.
Check each row has a baseline, a target, a source and a timeline.
Ask whether each target rests on evidence, such as comparable programme data.
worked_example.answer: Targets are Rs 16,000 more income (38.1%) and 10 points less poverty; both need evidence behind them.

mistakes: Listing activities as outputs, or outputs as outcomes.
Writing 'favourable policy environment' in the assumptions column with no specifics.
Using more than 5 to 7 indicators per level.
Collecting the baseline late, or with different tools from the endline.

recall.q: Who developed the logframe and when?
recall.a: Practical Concepts Inc. for USAID, in 1969.

recall.q: Where does the logframe logic become testable?
recall.a: In the assumptions column.

recall.q: What is the difference between a milestone and a target?
recall.a: A milestone is a qualitative marker; a target is a quantitative level for an indicator.

recall.q: When must a baseline be collected?
recall.a: Before the programme begins, using the same methods as the endline.

recall.q: What is the hybrid approach?
recall.a: A logframe for donor compliance plus a richer parallel system for learning.

sections.title: Indicators: Designing & Selecting
sections.big_idea: A good indicator says **who, what, how much and when**, and a good set is small enough to use.
in_plain_words: An indicator stands in for a result, so its quality limits your measurement. SMART gives a first screen, but you also need a precise definition, a numerator and denominator, planned disaggregation, a named source, and baseline and target values. Put all of that on a one-page reference sheet so every field team collects the same thing.

Choose fewer indicators and ask five questions of each, especially whether the data will be used. Beware of Goodhart's Law: **when a measure becomes a target it stops being a good measure**. Pair quantity with quality, verify without warning, and make honest reporting safe. Gender-responsive indicators go beyond counting women.

diagram.note: the deck's own percentage example; define both numbers exactly

key_terms.meaning: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound.
An observable stand-in for a harder concept.
Splitting data by gender, age, caste or geography, planned in advance.
A one-page definition of an indicator for all collectors.
A measure used as a target ceases to be a good measure.
A few indicators tracked continuously for early warning.

worked_example.title: Percentage and set size
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's SRI example: 300 farmers were trained and 250 now practise SRI. Then check the size of a minimum viable indicator set.
steps: Indicator = practising ÷ trained × 100.
250 ÷ 300 × 100 = 83.3 percent of trained farmers practise SRI.
Minimum viable set, lower end: 2 + 3 + 5 + 4 = 14.
Upper end: 3 + 4 + 7 + 6 = 20.
The deck warns that a framework over 30 will not be used well.
worked_example.answer: 83.3% practise SRI; a well-sized framework holds 14 to 20 indicators.

mistakes: Writing 'improved access to financial services' without defining access or who is covered.
Counting women's participation and calling it gender-responsive.
Adding indicators because someone asked, without checking they will inform a decision.
Making the staff who collect data answer for the numbers, which invites gaming.

recall.q: What do the five SMART letters stand for?
recall.a: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound.

recall.q: What must be specified for a percentage indicator?
recall.a: The numerator and the denominator exactly.

recall.q: Give one way to reduce gaming risk.
recall.a: Any one of: indicator combinations, quality alongside quantity, unannounced verification, separating collectors from accountability, and safe reporting.

recall.q: What size is the minimum viable indicator set?
recall.a: 14 to 20 indicators in total.

recall.q: Which two of the five selection questions decide whether to cut?
recall.a: Will this data be used for a decision, and what would we do differently with good or poor results.

sections.title: Data Collection Methods
sections.big_idea: Pick the method that fits the question and the setting, then protect the **quality, ethics and records** of what you collect.
in_plain_words: Surveys give numbers, qualitative methods give reasons, and participatory methods let communities speak for themselves. Check sampling, pilot the questionnaire and expect response bias, since people tend to please the organisation they depend on. Use FGDs for shared norms and individual interviews for sensitive topics.

Look at administrative data first, because India has a rich supply, and read its limits. Digital tools help in the field only if they work offline. **Quality control is routine**: training, back-checks, range checks and completeness checks. Consent must be informed and voluntary, and cleaning decisions must be logged.

key_terms.meaning: A guided group discussion of 6 to 8 people on shared norms.
An in-depth interview with someone holding specific knowledge.
Re-interviewing a sample of households to test consistency.
Answers shaped by what respondents think the organisation wants.
Understanding purpose, right to refuse, data use and access.
An interview completed without visiting the respondent.

worked_example.title: Plan a back-check
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a survey covers 400 households. The deck says a supervisor re-interviews 5 to 10% of surveyed households within 48 hours.
steps: Lower bound: 400 × 0.05 = 20 households.
Upper bound: 400 × 0.1 = 40 households.
Schedule each re-interview within 48 hours of the original visit.
Compare key responses for consistency and log any gaps.
Add GPS and audio checks if the survey is digital, as slide 39 recommends.
worked_example.answer: Re-interview between 20 and 40 households within 48 hours.

mistakes: Using an FGD for a shame-laden topic such as domestic violence. Use individual interviews instead.
Holding the FGD at the programme's venue, which suppresses criticism.
Treating administrative data as ground truth despite lags and over-reporting.
Hinting that benefits depend on answering a survey, which makes consent invalid.

recall.q: When should you use an IDI instead of an FGD?
recall.a: For sensitive topics, individual experiences, or when group pressure would suppress honest answers.

recall.q: Name two offline-capable tools from the deck.
recall.a: KoBoToolbox and ODK Collect.

recall.q: What are the five data quality dimensions?
recall.a: Validity, reliability, timeliness, precision and integrity.

recall.q: What does cleaning data involve beyond tidying?
recall.a: Analytical choices such as handling missing data and outliers, which must be documented in a log.

recall.q: What share of households does a back-check re-interview?
recall.a: 5 to 10%, within 48 hours.

sections.title: Evaluation Design
sections.big_idea: Start with the **question you need answered**, then choose the evaluation type and the design that can answer it.
in_plain_words: Evaluation covers very different questions: is the design right, is it being delivered as planned, did outcomes occur, did the programme cause them, was it good value, are we learning enough. Each has its own type and timing. Midterm evaluations work best when they look for evidence that the ToC is wrong.

Designs range from RCTs to pre-post comparisons. Quasi-experimental designs such as DiD, RDD, IV, PSM and synthetic control build a counterfactual without randomising. **A pre-post design shows change but cannot say why.** Process tracing and contribution analysis suit programmes with no counterfactual. Write a ToR with four to six specific questions.

key_terms.meaning: What would have happened without the programme.
Random assignment to treatment and control groups.
Comparing change over time between treatment and control groups.
The assumption both groups would have changed alike without the programme.
Testing the ToC's causal steps against observable evidence.
Terms of Reference: the brief that commissions an evaluation.

worked_example.title: Work out a DiD estimate
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: Phase 1 districts get the programme first, and Phase 2 districts are the comparison. Average income is 40 in both groups at baseline, in thousand rupees.
steps: Phase 1 ends at 52: change is 52 − 40 = 12.
Phase 2 ends at 46: change is 46 − 40 = 6.
The double difference is Phase 1 change minus Phase 2 change.
12 − 6 = 6, so the programme effect is 6 thousand rupees.
This holds only if the two groups would have changed alike without the programme.
worked_example.answer: DiD estimates an effect of 6 thousand rupees, valid if parallel trends hold.

mistakes: Using a pre-post survey for every question regardless of what you need to know.
Claiming causal impact from a design with no counterfactual.
Writing a vague evaluation question such as 'evaluate effectiveness'.
Treating a midterm as a mini-endline that records progress and challenges nothing.

recall.q: What does formative evaluation ask?
recall.a: How can we improve; its findings are used to change the programme.

recall.q: What is the key assumption of DiD?
recall.a: Parallel trends: both groups would have changed similarly without the programme.

recall.q: What is the fatal flaw of a pre-post design?
recall.a: It cannot separate programme effects from secular trends, seasons or other external changes.

recall.q: How many questions should a ToR contain?
recall.a: A maximum of four to six, each specific and answerable.

recall.q: What rule does the decision guide give for choosing methods?
recall.a: Choose your evaluation question before your method.

sections.title: Attribution & Contribution
sections.big_idea: Match your **causal claim to your design**: claim attribution only with a counterfactual, and otherwise tell an honest contribution story.
in_plain_words: Incomes may rise for reasons that have nothing to do with a programme, so a rise on its own proves little. Designs sit on a spectrum from RCTs, which support the strongest claims, to pre-post studies, which show change and cannot attribute it. Where many actors work together, claim contribution: show the ToC held, rule out alternatives and say what you cannot show.

Realist evaluation asks what works for whom and where. Systems change needs Outcome Harvesting. **Cost-effectiveness needs all costs and a comparison.** The OECD-DAC criteria give a shared checklist of questions, and sustainability is the one most often missed. Look for unintended effects, good and bad, and report negative or null findings candidly.

diagram.caption: the attribution spectrum, strongest claim at the top

key_terms.meaning: How far outcomes can be credited to the programme alone.
The programme's role alongside other factors.
Context plus mechanism gives outcome, in realist evaluation.
Cost-effectiveness: cost per unit of outcome.
Local elites taking benefits meant for marginalised people.
More of the intervention goes with more change.

worked_example.title: Cost per employed woman
worked_example.setup: The deck's example: a programme spends Rs 2 crore and 500 women complete training and are employed after one year. Compare it with an illustrative alternative.
steps: Rs 2 crore is 20,000,000 rupees.
Cost per employed woman: 20,000,000 ÷ 500 = 40,000.
Suppose an alternative costs Rs 50,000 per employed woman (illustrative).
The gap is 50,000 − 40,000 = 10,000 per woman.
The figure is only meaningful when quality and durability are comparable.
worked_example.answer: Rs 40,000 per employed woman; Rs 10,000 less than the illustrative alternative, if outcomes are comparable.

mistakes: Reading a 35% income rise as the programme effect with no comparison.
Computing CEA from direct activity costs only, leaving out staff and overheads.
Reporting only the best-performing subgroup as the overall result.
Hiding negative or null findings, which makes your positive findings less credible.

recall.q: What is a counterfactual?
recall.a: What would have happened to participants without the intervention.

recall.q: Name three kinds of evidence for a contribution case.
recall.a: Any three of: ToC held, alternatives addressed, beneficiary attribution, dose-response, timing.

recall.q: Which OECD-DAC criterion does the deck call most neglected?
recall.a: Sustainability.

recall.q: What does Outcome Harvesting do?
recall.a: It collects outcomes that occurred and works backwards to assess contribution.

recall.q: Why must CEA include staff and overhead costs?
recall.a: Leaving them out makes cost per outcome artificially low.

sections.title: Learning Systems & Adaptive Management
sections.big_idea: Learning needs **rhythm, authority and honesty**: regular reviews, permission to change, and safety to say what is not working.
in_plain_words: Learning is the least developed function of MEL. Evidence arrives late, poor results trigger defensiveness, there is rarely space for frank talk, staff turn over, and donors seldom fund learning. A learning system answers each with a review rhythm, learning events, documentation, decision protocols and knowledge management.

Adaptive management adds authority to change course. PDIA goes further, starting from a local problem and running quick experiments. Developmental evaluation embeds an evaluator in a changing programme. **Single-loop learning fixes the action; double-loop questions the strategy.** Add feedback mechanisms so communities can speak and see a response.

diagram.caption: the PDIA loop, run in weekly cycles

key_terms.meaning: Adjusting design and delivery in response to evidence.
USAID's Collaborating, Learning, Adapting framework.
Problem-Driven Iterative Adaptation, built on rapid experiments.
Correcting an error within existing norms.
Questioning the norms and strategy themselves.
An agreement on which evidence triggers which decision.

worked_example.title: Name the learning loop
worked_example.setup: Coverage in a programme is low. Three teams respond differently.
steps: Team A hires more field staff: it corrects the action within the same approach, so this is single loop.
Team B asks whether field-based delivery is the right model: it questions the strategy, so this is double loop.
Team C asks why the system never flagged low coverage early: it questions how the organisation learns, so this is triple loop.
Set a protocol that names the trigger, for example a coverage figure below the agreed level.
Say who convenes the review and by when.
worked_example.answer: A is single loop, B is double loop, C is triple loop.

mistakes: Treating learning as an annual event instead of a regular rhythm.
Needing donor approval for every adjustment, which makes adaptation costly.
Running a feedback mechanism that is never answered.
Scaling before you understand why an approach worked.

recall.q: What are the four parts of adaptive management?
recall.a: Regular evidence review, willingness to challenge assumptions, authority to change, and documentation of what changed and why.

recall.q: What does PDIA stand for?
recall.a: Problem-Driven Iterative Adaptation.

recall.q: What distinguishes double-loop from single-loop learning?
recall.a: Double-loop learning questions the norms and the strategy as well as the action.

recall.q: Name two knowledge management practices.
recall.a: Any two of: documentation, after-action reviews, learning notes, onboarding transfer, exit interviews, cross-programme learning.

recall.q: What makes a feedback mechanism functional?
recall.a: Accessible, confidential, responsive, disaggregated and integrated with MEL.

sections.title: Communicating Evidence
sections.big_idea: Write and show evidence for **the person who will use it**, and tell them plainly what the numbers say.
in_plain_words: Start with the user and the decision. A donor, a field team and a community each need a different format, length and language. Lead with findings, state significance directly, show uncertainty openly, and make recommendations specific and assigned to someone, with a date.

Charts persuade, so check them. **Start bars at zero**, avoid too many segments, plot rates on maps instead of raw counts, and show subgroups separately. Policy influence needs relationships built early, short briefs, framing around government priorities, watching for policy windows and coalitions. Evidence rarely drives policy alone.

diagram.caption: one body of findings, six formats

key_terms.meaning: Opens with findings and puts methods in an appendix.
A chart axis starting above zero, which inflates change.
A map shading regions by an indicator, best with rates.
A 2 to 4 page summary built for government readers.
A moment such as a budget cycle when evidence gets heard.
Evidence is one input beside politics and interests.

worked_example.title: Why the axis start matters
worked_example.setup: From the deck: a change from 40% to 44% is drawn on a bar chart whose axis runs from 38% to 46%, then on a 0 to 100% axis.
steps: The change is 44 − 40 = 4 points.
As a share of the starting value: 4 ÷ 40 = 10%.
On the 38 axis, bar heights above the axis are 40 − 38 = 2 and 44 − 38 = 6.
The 44 bar looks 6 ÷ 2 = 3 times taller than the 40 bar.
On a zero axis the ratio is 44 ÷ 40 = 1.1, a modest rise.
worked_example.answer: A 10% rise looks threefold on a truncated axis and 1.1 times on a zero axis.

mistakes: Writing recommendations such as 'strengthen community engagement' with no owner or date.
Starting the report with methodology instead of findings.
Averaging men's and women's outcomes into one bar.
Waiting until the evaluation ends to talk to government officials.

recall.q: What should a MEL report lead with?
recall.a: Findings, with methods in an appendix.

recall.q: What is the non-zero baseline error?
recall.a: Starting a bar chart's axis above zero, which makes small changes look dramatic.

recall.q: Which format suits field teams?
recall.a: A visual one-pager, a verbal debrief and a local-language summary.

recall.q: Name two evidence-to-policy tactics.
recall.a: Any two of: build relationships early, frame around government priorities, policy-ready formats, identify policy windows, build coalitions.

recall.q: Why show disaggregation visually?
recall.a: Averaging hides systematic exclusion, and side-by-side bars make it legible.

sections.title: MEL in Practice: Common Failures
sections.big_idea: Most MEL failures repeat: **designed late, no baseline, too many indicators, outputs called outcomes, data unused** and a culture that punishes honesty.
in_plain_words: The ten failures fall into design, use and learning. Design failures are late MEL, no baseline, indicator overload and mislabelled outputs. Use failures are data nobody uses and findings ignored. Learning failures are unaddressed disaggregation, no lessons from failure, MEL owned by one officer, and compliance taking the place of learning.

Many of these trace to culture more than skill. In a healthy culture leaders say what is not working and staff report problems without fear. In a compliance culture reports go to donors and are filed. **Technical fixes are easier than cultural change**, but lasting improvement lives in culture.

left.title: Healthy MEL culture
items: Leaders say what is not working
Negative findings come with a response
MEL is discussed at all-staff meetings

right.title: Compliance MEL culture
items: Data collection seen as extra burden
Staff afraid to report missed targets

key_terms.meaning: So many indicators that data cannot be used.
MEL added after the programme starts.
A system built only around donor reporting.
A system built to improve the programme.
Breaking data into subgroups to reveal exclusion.
A documented lesson from a programme that did not work.

worked_example.title: Score a framework against the diagnostic
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a framework has 42 indicators, a baseline collected 8 months after launch, and only training counts at outcome level.
steps: Indicators: the diagnostic flags more than 30 and prefers under 20.
To reach the top of the 14 to 20 range, cut 42 − 20 = 22 indicators.
Baseline: 6 months or more after start is a red flag, so 8 months fails.
Outcome level holds only outputs, which is a red flag on question 4.
Plan fixes: reduce the set, add outcome indicators, and record the baseline gap.
worked_example.answer: Three red flags; cutting 22 indicators gets the set to the upper limit of the good range.

mistakes: Treating MEL as the MEL officer's job alone.
Writing an evaluation action plan with no owner, so findings are ignored.
Hiding failures instead of recording lessons from them.
Reporting only aggregate data and missing who is excluded.

recall.q: Name two of the five failures on slide 74.
recall.a: Any two of: MEL designed late, no baseline, indicator overload, outputs reported as outcomes, data collected but unused.

recall.q: Which failure does the deck call the most expensive?
recall.a: Evaluation findings ignored.

recall.q: What does a compliance MEL culture look like?
recall.a: Reports written for donors, data collection seen as burden, findings filed, staff afraid to report missed targets.

recall.q: Why is MEL owned by one person a failure?
recall.a: Programme staff do not own the data or integrate learning.

recall.q: What did the culture quote say about MEL systems?
recall.a: Culture eats strategy for breakfast, and it eats MEL systems for lunch.

sections.title: MEL for Different Contexts
sections.big_idea: The principles hold everywhere, but the **tools must be proportionate** to the speed, scale and politics of the setting.
in_plain_words: Humanitarian work is fast and insecure: baselines are often impossible, people move, and accountability to affected people matters most. Use rapid assessments for operations, real-time monitoring and the humanitarian minimum standards as benchmarks. Advocacy is slow and shared, so track milestones, influence and implementation instead of counting briefs.

Small NGOs need a **minimum viable MEL**: a one-page ToC, a handful of indicators, a light baseline, quarterly reviews and one learning note. Government programmes work at huge scale with political pressure to report success, but offer rich MIS data. In each context ask what the setting changes about speed, attribution and honesty.

key_terms.meaning: Monitoring, Evaluation, Accountability, Learning.
Benchmarks for water, food, shelter and health in a crisis.
Tracking relationships with key decision-makers over time.
Checking whether adopted policies are implemented.
The national citizen grievance system run by DARPG.
A ranking of districts on 49 indicators across 5 sectors.

worked_example.title: Pick an approach for each case
worked_example.setup: Three organisations ask for advice: a flood-response agency, a group running a ten-year policy campaign, and a small NGO with no MEL staff.
steps: Flood response: use rapid needs assessment, real-time monitoring and minimum-standard benchmarks, since no baseline exists.
Policy campaign: track milestones, map influence, monitor implementation and write a contribution narrative.
Small NGO: apply the six-part minimum, with a one-page ToC and 5 to 8 indicators.
Add feedback mechanisms to each, so affected people can respond.
Match the effort to capacity, never to what looks most rigorous.
worked_example.answer: Rapid and real-time for the flood, milestones and influence for the campaign, minimum viable MEL for the small NGO.

mistakes: Transplanting stable-setting survey methods into a crisis.
Counting policy briefs as proof that advocacy is working.
Building a 50-indicator logframe for a small NGO.
Treating government MIS figures as ground truth despite over-reporting incentives.

recall.q: What does the A in MEAL add?
recall.a: Accountability, recognising feedback mechanisms as a core function.

recall.q: What do humanitarian minimum standards provide?
recall.a: Minimum standards (water, food, shelter, health) as benchmarks without a full baseline.

recall.q: Name two advocacy MEL approaches.
recall.a: Any two of: milestones tracking, influence mapping, policy monitoring, Most Significant Change, contribution narrative.

recall.q: What is in minimum viable MEL for a small NGO?
recall.a: A one-page ToC, 5 to 8 indicators, a baseline, quarterly review, annual reflection and one learning note.

recall.q: Where does advocacy often fall short?
recall.a: In the gap between policy adoption and implementation.

sections.title: Further Reading & Resources
sections.big_idea: The last section is a **toolkit**: reading, vocabulary, tools by stage, open data, checklists and samples you can reuse.
in_plain_words: Use the reading list in three tiers: ToC and planning, impact evaluation, and India-specific sources. The vocabulary table fixes twenty terms, and the tools table maps each MEL stage to free resources. India's open data, from NFHS to UDISE+, can cut the cost of baselines when you read its limits.

The supplementary slides add practice. The self-assessment and ten-question diagnostic let you judge yourself and a programme. The sample logframe, MEL plan and ToR show finished documents. Gender, ethics, evidence use and capacity building round out the list. **Reuse the samples as templates** and adapt them to your own programme.

key_terms.meaning: Development Monitoring and Evaluation Office under NITI Aayog.
A free database of evaluation methods and tools.
A village-level socioeconomic dataset for India.
Women's Empowerment in Agriculture Index, five domains.
Ethics committee approval for research with people.
Measures how people divide productive and care work.

worked_example.title: Size a MEL budget from the sample plan
worked_example.setup: The sample programme has a Rs 4.2 crore budget over 4 years, with MEL at 7%. The sample ToR gives an evaluation budget of Rs 18 lakh (an assumption: it is paid from the MEL line).
steps: MEL budget in crore: 4.2 × 0.07 = 0.294.
In lakh (100 lakh to a crore): 0.294 × 100 = 29.4.
Evaluation share: 18 ÷ 29.4 = 61.2%.
That leaves 29.4 − 18 = 11.4 lakh for baseline, monitoring and learning.
Check whether the remaining amount covers the data collection in the MEL plan.
worked_example.answer: MEL budget is Rs 29.4 lakh; the endline evaluation takes about 61%, leaving Rs 11.4 lakh.

mistakes: Reading only one tier of the reading list and missing the RCT critique.
Treating open data sources as ground truth without reading their limits.
Sending one officer on a course and expecting organisational capacity.
Copying the sample logframe without adapting it to your own ToC.

recall.q: Which paper is the key RCT critique in the reading list?
recall.a: Deaton and Cartwright (2018), 'Understanding and Misunderstanding Randomized Controlled Trials'.

recall.q: Name two free India data sources.
recall.a: Any two of: data.gov.in, MoSPI, NFHS, SHRUG, UDISE+, HMIS.

recall.q: What are the five WEAI domains?
recall.a: Decisions about agriculture, access to resources, control of income, leadership and time allocation.

recall.q: What does the training-only trap say?
recall.a: Sending one officer on a course does not build organisational MEL capacity without systems, time and leadership.

recall.q: Name two core ethical principles of evaluation.
recall.a: Any two of: respect for persons, beneficence, justice, independence, transparency.

notes.2: Treat this agenda as the map. Twelve sections run from definitions to the reading list, and the slides after 89 add extra tools and samples. If your time is short, read sections 1, 2 and 4 first, because every later section leans on them.
notes.4: Keep the three letters in sequence: monitoring collects, evaluation judges, learning acts. Each one fails without the one before it, and the last box warns that reports nobody acts on are the usual result. **Treat MEL as one system** that runs from data to decision.
notes.5: Four functions pull in four directions. Accountability looks up to funders, management looks at this month, learning looks at the next programme. The tension to remember is that **a system built mainly for donors produces flattering data**. Ask which function each report you write is serving.
notes.6: Read the table as a list of fashions, each leaving a tool behind. The logframe dates to 1969 and was built for infrastructure. When you pick up any tool, **ask what it was designed for** and whether your programme looks like that. The DMEO box gives you a public source for Indian scheme evaluations.
notes.7: Each funder in the table asks for something different, so one programme can owe three sets of numbers. Before you design indicators, **list your funders and what each wants**. The FCRA paragraph shows the mix moving towards domestic funders, whose demands differ from international donors.
notes.8: Memorise the chain as five words: inputs, activities, outputs, outcomes, impact. The line that matters is where programme control ends, after outputs. **Monitoring watches the left half, evaluation the right half.** Use the farm example whenever you need to explain the chain to someone new.
notes.9: An output says what you did and an outcome says what changed. Apply the 'so what?' test to any indicator and keep asking until the answer is about people's lives. If a row in your report stops at a count of sessions, **you are still at output level**.
notes.10: Five components, each feeding the next, starting with the ToC. The one people skip is the MEL plan, the document naming every indicator's source, tool, owner and frequency. Design MEL **before the programme starts**, and budget for it: the slide gives 5 to 10% of programme budget as the norm, rising to 12 to 15% where learning ambitions are high.
notes.12: A ToC is a hypothesis, so it can be wrong. Write it as if, then, because, and **spend your effort on the because**, which is the assumption. Use the seven ingredients as a checklist when you review someone's ToC: problem, hypothesis, pathways, assumptions, boundaries, stakeholders, preconditions.
notes.13: For each arrow in a results chain, ask what must be true for it to work, then ask whether you have evidence or only hope. The three Indian examples show that **failing assumptions are usually social**, such as who controls money or who maintains a pump. Use the table to pick a test for each type.
notes.14: The five steps run from the problem to regular revision. Process matters: who sits in the room decides whether the ToC guides work. Note the ordering rule, **ToC first, logframe second**. The weaknesses paragraph is a ready list of what to look for when you read a proposal.
notes.15: A linear chain suits complicated problems such as a bridge. Reducing domestic violence or improving governance is complex, so the same input can lead to different results. In that case **ask for contribution, track context and revise often**. PDIA and developmental evaluation come later for exactly these cases.
notes.16: Compare the two girls' education ToCs line by line. The weak one jumps from school attendance to economic participation. The strong one names two barriers, states its assumptions and admits what it cannot control. **Use the strong version as a template** when you write your own.
notes.17: Choose the mechanism before the intervention. The table lists five: information, incentives, norms, power and systems, and each needs different measurement. The warning at the bottom is the one to keep: **an information campaign cannot fix a problem caused by food insecurity or lack of decision power**.
notes.18: Use this slide as a review sheet. Count the strong signs a ToC shows, then count its red flags. A blank assumptions box, or outputs labelled as outcomes, **should stop you at once**. The closing paragraph asks you to revisit the ToC at least once a year.
notes.20: Read the logframe in two directions. Down the columns is vertical logic: if activities happen and assumptions hold, outputs follow. Along each row is horizontal logic: result, indicator, source. **The assumptions column is where the logic becomes testable**, and it is the one most often left blank.
notes.21: Donors draw the same logic in different shapes. The table lets you translate between them, so learn the two you meet most often. Read the indicator fatigue paragraph too: 50 to 100 indicators leave **no time for analysis**, which makes limiting indicators a core skill.
notes.22: A workplan says how and when, and the MEL plan says what data, by whom. Keep them aligned, or the MEL plan collects data nobody needs. Use the milestone and target distinction: **a target counts something, a milestone describes a condition**. Put baseline, midline and endline in the workplan with budgets.
notes.23: Learn the critique so you can use the tool better. The five criticisms share a root: the logframe assumes you know the outcomes in advance. The hybrid approach is the practical answer. **Run the logframe for the funder and a richer system for the team**, and budget the extra effort.
notes.24: This matrix adds baseline, target and timeline columns to the results chain. Check that every row has all three. Adoption is an intermediate outcome. Without a starting value you cannot show change, and targets need evidence behind them. **Targets that are always met or never met both signal a design problem.**
notes.25: A baseline must come before the programme and use the same instruments as the endline. Check four things: all outcome indicators are covered, a comparison group is measured at the same time, disaggregation matches the endline, and the sample can detect change. **A late baseline measures a programme already underway.**
notes.26: Use the table as a seven-line audit of a results framework. For each row, hold the quality standard against the common failure and mark where yours falls. The last paragraph is the safeguard: **treat the framework as provisional** and schedule a formal review at midterm.
notes.28: An indicator is a stand-in for a result, so your measurement is only as good as it. Screen with SMART, then walk the anatomy list: name, definition, numerator and denominator, disaggregation, source, baseline and target. **Write a one-page reference sheet per indicator** so every field team collects it the same way.
notes.29: Pick the indicator type by what you need to learn. Quantitative says how much, qualitative says why and for whom, proxy stands in for something hard to see, process checks delivery, sentinel gives early warning. The ANC example warns that **a proxy works only if it leads to the outcome**.
notes.30: Counting women in a programme does not show whether it changed their lives. The disaggregation fallacy paragraph lists the questions to ask instead: equal access, decision-making power, extra time burden. The right-hand column shows how to **rewrite a standard indicator so it measures women's control** as well as presence.
notes.31: Choosing indicators means cutting. Put each proposed indicator through the five questions, and drop any where you cannot answer the third (will it be used) and the fifth (what would we do differently). The chart is marked illustrative, so **do not quote it as a published study**.
notes.32: Standard indicators let you compare with others, and custom ones fit your own mechanism. Use the two boxes as a decision rule: standard when benchmarks or donors require them, custom when your pathway is unusual. The table names Indian sources such as NFHS, UDISE+ and ASER **to check before you invent a new indicator**.
notes.33: Goodhart's Law says that once a measure becomes a target, people aim at the measure. All three examples hit their numbers and missed their purpose. Pair quantity with quality, verify without warning, and **make bad numbers safe to report**, since fear of consequences pushes teams to hide problems.
notes.34: Compare the good and weak indicators: the good ones say who, what, how and when. The minimum viable set is 14 to 20 indicators, and above 30 the slide warns they will not be used well. If a donor demands more, **negotiate, or run a light internal set alongside**.
notes.36: Surveys are common and easy to get wrong. Check the five questionnaire rules, then read the response bias paragraph: people tell the NGO they depend on what it wants to hear. Pick a sampling method by asking what list you hold. **Pilot with 10 to 20 respondents** before full roll-out.
notes.37: Match the method to the topic. FGDs suit shared norms and fail on shame-laden topics, where individual interviews are right. The rural India paragraph gives practical rules: separate groups by caste and gender, explain confidentiality, use a note-taker, and **hold the session away from the programme's own venue**.
notes.38: These methods let communities do the assessing. Read the table as a menu: maps, calendars, trend lines, Venn diagrams and Most Significant Change. MSC uses panels to choose among collected stories and surfaces unexpected effects. **Participation counts only if communities can decide what gets measured.**
notes.39: Choose a tool by connectivity first. In parts of Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh and eastern UP, offline-first tools such as KoBoToolbox and ODK are essential. Digital collection brings new fraud risks, such as porch surveys. **Keep GPS checks, audio samples and supervisor spot-checks** even when the data is digital.
notes.40: Before you collect anything, check what already exists. The four boxes name sources with free data. Use administrative data for baselines, trends, comparisons and corroboration. Then **read the limitations paragraph**: over-reporting incentives, data lags of three years or more, and thin coverage below district level.
notes.41: Data quality has five dimensions: validity, reliability, timeliness, precision and integrity. Name the dimension each check protects when you design it. Back-checks of 5 to 10% of households within 48 hours are the most practical control. **Poor data is worse than none** because it creates false confidence.
notes.42: Consent must be informed and voluntary, so never hint that benefits depend on answering. Watch small cells: two Dalit women in a group of fifty can be identified without a name. The DPDP Act paragraph gives a date, so **check your legal duties before you store respondent data**. Share findings back with communities.
notes.43: Follow the five steps in order and keep a cleaning log. Cleaning decisions are analytical choices, so write each one down. The tools paragraph is reassuring: Excel used well handles most NGO analysis. **Rigour and documentation matter more than the software** you choose.
notes.45: Start from the question, then pick the evaluation type. The table pairs each type with its question and its timing. Notice that most evaluations try to be formative and summative at once and end up neither. **A good midterm hunts for evidence that the ToC is wrong.**
notes.46: The RCT's strength is the counterfactual: a randomised control group shows what would have happened anyway. Its limits are cost, ethics, scale and generalising. **A result from one population and place does not carry over automatically.** Read Deaton and Cartwright, named on the slide, for the critique.
notes.47: You will rarely run these designs yourself, yet you should recognise them. DiD compares change in two groups and needs parallel trends, and a phased rollout gives you a natural use. The key message: **know whether a finding is a correlation or a causal estimate** before you quote it.
notes.48: Most evaluations here have no counterfactual and can still be honest. A pre-post design shows change but cannot tell you why it happened. Process tracing tests the ToC step by step, and contribution analysis follows five steps. **State exactly what your design can and cannot claim.**
notes.49: A ToR decides whether an evaluation is useful. Cover context, purpose, questions, design, data and deliverables. Keep to four to six questions, each answerable and tied to a decision. On internal versus external, **the slide recommends an external evaluator working closely with your MEL team**.
notes.50: Use the table to go from question to design: ask the question first, then read across to the method. The closing paragraph is the rule of the whole section: **choose your question before your method**. A pre-post survey cannot say whether the programme caused anything. The chart is illustrative.
notes.52: Incomes rising 35% tells you something happened, and it does not tell you why. The attribution spectrum ranks designs from RCT down to pre-post. Place your own evaluation on it before you write conclusions. **Without a comparison group, a before-after change is a correlation.**
notes.53: Contribution is the honest claim when many actors work in one area. Build the case from five kinds of evidence: the ToC held, alternatives addressed, participants credit the programme, dose-response, and timing. The example sentence shows how to **write the claim with its limits attached**.
notes.54: Realist evaluation asks what works, for whom, where and why. Learn the CMO configuration: context triggers a mechanism that produces an outcome. In the microfinance example the mechanism was peer accountability, present where SHGs already existed. **An average across districts would have hidden that finding.**
notes.55: Systems change moves rules, markets and norms, so logframe indicators miss it. Outcome Harvesting collects changes in actors' behaviour first and works backwards to your contribution. Use the table to choose an approach for policy, market, norm, power or institutional change, and **expect long timelines**.
notes.56: CEA gives cost per unit of outcome and CBA puts a money value on outcomes. Work the example: ₹2 crore for 500 employed women is ₹40,000 each. That figure means little alone, so **always compare with an alternative**. The error list warns against counting only direct costs.
notes.57: The six criteria are a checklist for evaluation questions: relevance, coherence, effectiveness, efficiency, impact and sustainability. Not all six suit every evaluation, so choose by the decision at hand. Give sustainability extra attention, since it is **the weakest element in most programmes**, and plan for it from the start.
notes.58: Every programme has side effects. The table sorts them into positive, negative, displacement, dependency and elite capture. To find them, ask open questions at endline, run trust-building FGDs, use Outcome Harvesting and keep **a feedback line people can use safely**. A programme that measures only its targets cannot see harm.
notes.59: This is the section's summary. Match your causal claim to your design, prefer contribution framing when attribution is impossible, look for unintended effects, and plan for sustainability and cost data from the start. The closing paragraph argues that **candid reporting of failures makes your successes believable**.
notes.61: Learning is the weakest of the three functions. The five reasons it is hard are mostly organisational: late evidence, defensiveness, no space for honesty, turnover and no funding. Build the five components, especially the **decision protocol**, which fixes in advance which evidence triggers which action.
notes.62: Adaptive management is the L in MEL turned into practice. It needs four conditions: regular evidence review, willingness to challenge assumptions, authority to change, and documentation. If every change needs a long approval chain, **the learning has nowhere to go**. CLA is USAID's version.
notes.63: PDIA starts with a local problem and iterates. Compare the two models: the traditional one plans, implements and evaluates, while PDIA loops through problem, iterate, learn and adapt. Learning cycles run weekly. **Do not scale until you understand what you are scaling.**
notes.64: Developmental evaluation fits programmes still taking shape: innovation, complex systems, scaling and crisis. The evaluator sits inside the team and helps work out the criteria as they learn. Not every funder accepts it in place of logframe-based MEL, so **raise it early in negotiations**.
notes.65: The three loops go deeper each time. Single loop fixes the action, double loop questions the strategy, triple loop questions how you learn. Use the coverage example to practise telling them apart. Organisations stay at single loop because deeper questions put leaders at risk. **Invite challenge and protect those who raise it.**
notes.66: People leave, and learning leaves with them. The slide quotes turnover of 40 to 60% in some studies. The six practices are your toolkit: documentation, after-action reviews, learning notes, onboarding, exit interviews and cross-programme sharing. **Pick the one your team has none of and start there.**
notes.67: Feedback without a response is not accountability. The ALNAP findings say mechanisms are rarely designed with communities and rarely used to change anything. Check yours against five tests: accessible, confidential, responsive, disaggregated, integrated with MEL. **Track who uses it**, so you can see whom it misses.
notes.69: Write for the decision-maker. Put findings first, state significance directly, show uncertainty plainly and make recommendations specific and assigned. The example recommendation names a team, a revision and a quarter. **A report with no negative findings is not credible.**
notes.70: Check each chart against the misuse column. The non-zero baseline is the one to remember: a 4-point change on a 38 to 46 axis looks dramatic. **Draw bars from zero.** Then show subgroups separately, since an average hides exclusion.
notes.71: The same findings need six formats. Choose from the table by asking what each audience will do with the result. Donors want framework alignment, leaders want decisions, field teams want a local one-pager and communities want to be heard. **Take findings back to communities in their own language.**
notes.72: Evidence does not speak for itself. Policy follows politics, interests and timing. Use the five tactics: build relationships early, frame around government priorities, produce short briefs, watch for policy windows and **work in coalitions**. An 80-page report is a poor tool for this job.
notes.74: Read failures one to five as a design checklist: late MEL, no baseline, too many indicators, outputs called outcomes, and unused data. The fifth sets a rule: **decide how data will be used before you collect it**. Mark which of these five your own programme is most at risk of.
notes.75: Failures six to ten are about use and culture. The costliest is an ignored evaluation, since the money was spent for no benefit. The slide says disaggregation is not optional. Number nine matters for your role: **MEL needs whole-team ownership**, so spread it beyond one officer.
notes.76: Many failures are cultural. Compare the two lists: a healthy culture discusses what is not working in public, and a compliance culture files reports. Use them as a diagnostic at your next team meeting. **Fixing culture is slower than fixing tools**, and it is where lasting change comes from.
notes.78: Humanitarian MEL adapts to speed and insecurity. A baseline is often impossible and people keep moving. Accountability joins the acronym as MEAL. Use rapid assessments for operational choices and never for impact claims, and **use the humanitarian minimum standards as benchmarks when a baseline is missing**.
notes.79: Advocacy results are slow and shared among many actors, so a count of policy briefs says little. The five approaches track milestones, relationships and implementation. Remember that adoption is not the finish line: **the gap between adoption and implementation** is where advocacy often falls short.
notes.80: A small NGO needs a proportionate system. The six-part minimum fits into normal operations: a one-page ToC, 5 to 8 indicators, a light baseline, quarterly review, annual reflection and one learning note. **The free resources in the table cover tools and evidence** at no cost.
notes.81: Scale and politics shape government MEL: the slide notes pressure to report success and a blurred line between accountability and performance. Use the MIS list as sources, with their known flaws in mind. MGNREGS data carries over-reporting incentives yet **still shows trends**. Read the repeal note before you cite it.
notes.83: Use the reading list in three tiers: ToC and planning, impact evaluation, and India-specific sources. Start with the free items, such as Gertler's book, the DMEO evaluations and BetterEvaluation. **Read Deaton and Cartwright beside Banerjee and Duflo** to hear both sides of the RCT argument.
notes.84: Twenty terms across two tables. Cover the right column and try to define each term before you look. Master four first: counterfactual, attribution, contribution and baseline, because **most of the arguments in this deck rest on them**.
notes.85: Match your stage to the tool. The table runs from design to learning, and each row names free resources. Design is 'non-negotiable' before programme start. Note that the midterm sits at Year 2 of a four-year programme. **Print it and mark the stage you are in.**
notes.86: Open data can replace costly primary collection. Start at data.gov.in and MoSPI, then move to the sector dashboards for employment, schools and health. BHUVAN adds a map layer. **Revisit the limitations on slide 40** before relying on any of these as ground truth.
notes.87: The table shows four career levels and the skills each needs. The skills gap paragraph lists four abilities (quantitative, qualitative, programmatic and communication) and says most people are strong on one or two. **Pick the weakest of the four and plan how to build it.**
notes.88: Six trends, each with a catch. AI raises consent and bias questions, real-time feedback raises response capacity, open data rewards honesty about negatives, and climate disruption needs its own baseline. Read the slide for **the question your organisation is likely to face first**.
notes.89: Use this as a self-assessment: tick what you can do at each level. If you cannot yet do the foundation items, return to sections 1 to 4. **Be honest about the level you are at.** The next step named on the slide is the MEL flagship course.
notes.90: Ten questions give a fast read on any MEL system. Score each as a red flag or a good sign. Questions 5 and 10 are about use: who acts on monitoring data, and when did evidence last change the programme? **If you cannot give an example, you have your answer.**
notes.91: Study a finished logframe against slide 20. Read along the Purpose row: the outcome statement, three indicators, sources and assumptions. Notice the assumptions are specific, such as childcare and mobility. **Check that each indicator has a named source**, then compare with the seven classic errors.
notes.92: The MEL plan turns the logframe into daily work. Each row gives definition, baseline, targets, source, frequency and owner. Read the 'own enterprise' row: the definition requires positive revenue for 3 or more consecutive months. **A definition this exact lets different staff collect the same figure.**
notes.93: The slide points to three flagship courses. Pick by need: MEL for deeper methods, data visualisation for presenting evidence, development economics for the theory that makes findings interpretable. Treat this 101 as the first step, since each of those courses goes further.
notes.94: A gender toolkit in one table. The five tools suit different settings: WEAI for agriculture, GiHA for emergencies, Gender at Work for rights programmes, SoNA for norms, EMERGE for survey measures. Time use data adds a missing piece. **Use women enumerators and women-only groups for sensitive topics.**
notes.95: Evaluation holds power over framing, voice and reporting. The five principles are respect, beneficence, justice, independence and transparency. Watch the commissioner's influence problem: evaluators paid by the programme feel pressure towards positive findings. **Name that pressure and resist it**, and know when IRB or IEC approval applies.
notes.96: Start from existing evidence before you design. The portals listed (3ie, Campbell, J-PAL and DevDiscourses) are free places to look. Ask the four questions on the slide about approaches, mechanisms, challenges and realistic levels. **Evidence from another country gives signals, and your context decides.**
notes.97: Training one officer does not build capacity. Use the table to work at three levels: individual skills, team habits, organisational systems. The four conditions listed (leadership, time, systems, funding) make training stick. The budgeting paragraph gives **5%, 7 to 10% and 12 to 15%** by complexity; compare slide 10.
notes.98: This bubble chart places methods on rigour, feasibility and cost. RCTs sit high on rigour and low on feasibility. DiD, RDD and PSM are the practical middle. **Match the method to the question**, and use the chart as a first filter when you decide what you can afford.
notes.99: The chord chart pairs indicator types with methods. Inputs and outputs use routine records, outcomes need surveys plus qualitative work, and impact needs a counterfactual. The logframe gap is the link between outcomes and credible measurement. **Name your method before you write an outcome indicator.**
notes.100: Use this sample ToR as a template. It runs through eight sections and shows how a specific decision shapes everything, from the questions to the comparison group. Count the questions: five, inside the four to six rule. **Notice the ethics section**, which requires women enumerators and consent.
notes.101: The closing slide says the gap between MEL spending and learning is cultural. It lists five conditions: leaders who use evidence, funders who reward honesty, practitioners who push back, communities with data, and MEL seen as service. **Pick one you can influence this year.**
notes.102: Failures live in the arrows. Look at the schematic and ask what must hold for each link. MEL's job is to test the links with evidence as well as count the boxes. Pair it with the assumption audit from slide 13 and **run it on your own programme**.
notes.103: A RACI matrix names who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed for each MEL task. Draw one before the programme starts, so ownership is clear before disputes appear. In the example, **field teams collect the data and officers answer for the reporting**.
